ESCHEAT OF A DECEDENT'S ESTATE TO THE STATE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · March 14, 2026

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's law on escheat of a decedent's estate to the state — Probate Code Part 4 (commencing with Section 6800) and the related unclaimed-property provisions of Code of Civil Procedure Title 10, Part 3 — as it may bear on the estate of Jordan Alex Lee (date of death: March 14, 2026; character and estimated value of estate property: Approximately $85,000 in bank accounts and personal property). It states what this law provides in general. It does not determine whether Jordan Alex Lee's estate has any heirs or devisees under California law, whether any escheat proceeding has been or will be commenced regarding this estate, or what a court would decide in a particular case, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about this estate's own facts.

WHEN A DECEDENT'S PROPERTY ESCHEATS
Under Probate Code Section 6800(a), a decedent's property escheats to the State of California — automatically, at the moment of death, without anyone having to petition for it — only if two conditions are both met: no one takes the property by testate succession (that is, there is no valid will disposing of it, or the will fails to dispose of it), and no one other than a government or governmental subdivision or agency takes it by intestate succession under the law of this state or any other jurisdiction. This rule applies whether or not the decedent was domiciled in California. Section 6800(b) then subjects escheated property to the same charges and trusts it would have carried had it passed by succession, and separately makes it subject to the unclaimed-property provisions of Code of Civil Procedure Title 10 (commencing with Section 1300) governing escheated estates — the procedural framework described in the rest of this sheet.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If a decedent, whether or not the decedent was domiciled in this state, leaves no one to take the decedent’s estate or any portion thereof by testate succession, and no one other than a government or governmental subdivision or agency to take the estate or a portion thereof by intestate succession, under the laws of this state or of any other jurisdiction, the same escheats at the time of the decedent’s death in accordance with this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6800(a) (California Legislative Information text), Probate Code, general escheat trigger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6800.)
  "Property that escheats to the state under this part, whether held by the state or its officers, is subject to the same charges and trusts to which it would have been subject if it had passed by succession and is also subject to the provisions of Title 10 (commencing with Section 1300) of Part 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure relating to escheated estates."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6800(b) (California Legislative Information text), Probate Code, subject to CCP Title 10 (this is subdivision (b) of the same Section 6800 quoted immediately above, not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6800.)
  Known gap: Section 6800(a) states the trigger in the abstract; it does not itself determine, for any particular decedent, whether every possible taker under California's intestate succession statutes (Probate Code Sections 6400-6455) and every other jurisdiction's law has in fact been exhausted — that determination depends on the specific family and property facts of the estate, which this sheet does not evaluate.

REAL PROPERTY AND TANGIBLE PERSONAL PROPERTY
California's escheat statute assigns different property types to the state under different tests. Real property located in California escheats to California under Probate Code Section 6801. Tangible personal property escheats to California under Section 6802 if it was customarily kept in California before the decedent's death, regardless of where it is located at death. A related but separate rule in Section 6803(a) reaches tangible personal property that is subject to the control of a California superior court for purposes of probate administration, but Section 6803(b) carves out an exception: that property goes to another jurisdiction instead, if that jurisdiction claims it and establishes that it is entitled to the property under its own law, that the decedent customarily kept the property there, and that California would have the reciprocal right to claim tangible property being administered in that jurisdiction if the decedent had customarily kept it in California.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Real property in this state escheats to this state in accordance with Section 6800."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6801 (California Legislative Information text), Probate Code, real property escheat (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6801.)
  "All tangible personal property owned by the decedent, wherever located at the decedent’s death, that was customarily kept in this state prior to the decedent’s death, escheats to this state in accordance with Section 6800."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6802 (California Legislative Information text), Probate Code, tangible personal property customarily kept in California (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6802.)
  "(a) Subject to subdivision (b), all tangible personal property owned by the decedent that is subject to the control of a superior court of this state for purposes of administration under this code escheats to this state in accordance with Section 6800."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6803(a) (California Legislative Information text), Probate Code, tangible personal property under California probate administration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6803.)
  "(1) The other jurisdiction is entitled to the property under its law. (2) The decedent customarily kept the property in that jurisdiction prior to the decedent’s death. (3) This state has the right to escheat and take tangible personal property being administered as part of a decedent’s estate in that jurisdiction if the decedent customarily kept the property in this state prior to the decedent’s death."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6803(b) (California Legislative Information text), Probate Code, reciprocal other-jurisdiction exception (this is subdivision (b) of the same Section 6803 quoted immediately above, not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6803.)
  Known gap: Sections 6801-6803 do not define 'customarily kept' or resolve close cases (property that moved between states, or was kept in more than one place) — nor do they say how a competing jurisdiction's claim under Section 6803(b) is to be adjudicated procedurally; this sheet does not apply these tests to any specific item of property.

INTANGIBLE PROPERTY
Intangible property (such as bank accounts, securities, or contract rights) is governed by domicile rather than by where the asset is physically kept. Under Probate Code Section 6804, intangible property owned by the decedent escheats to California only if the decedent was domiciled in California at death. Section 6805(a) separately reaches intangible property subject to the control of a California superior court for purposes of probate administration, and does so whether or not the decedent was domiciled in California — but Section 6805(b) carves out the same kind of reciprocal exception found in Section 6803(b): the property instead goes to another jurisdiction that claims it and establishes entitlement under its own law, the decedent's domicile there at death, and California's reciprocal right to intangible property administered there if the decedent had instead been domiciled in California.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "All intangible property owned by the decedent escheats to this state in accordance with Section 6800 if the decedent was domiciled in this state at the time of the decedent’s death."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6804 (California Legislative Information text), Probate Code, intangible property and domicile (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6804.)
  "(a) Subject to subdivision (b), all intangible property owned by the decedent that is subject to the control of a superior court of this state for purposes of administration under this code escheats to this state in accordance with Section 6800 whether or not the decedent was domiciled in this state at the time of the decedent’s death."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6805(a) (California Legislative Information text), Probate Code, intangible property under California probate administration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6805.)
  "(1) The other jurisdiction is entitled to the property under its laws. (2) The decedent was domiciled in that jurisdiction at the time of the decedent’s death. (3) This state has the right to escheat and take intangible property being administered as part of a decedent’s estate in that jurisdiction if the decedent was domiciled in this state at the time of the decedent’s death."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6805(b) (California Legislative Information text), Probate Code, reciprocal other-jurisdiction exception (this is subdivision (b) of the same Section 6805 quoted immediately above, not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6805.)
  Known gap: These sections turn on 'domicile,' a legal concept the statute does not define here and that can be genuinely contested where a decedent had connections to more than one state; this sheet does not determine any decedent's domicile.

CARVE-OUT FOR EMPLOYEE BENEFIT PLAN TRUSTS AND FUNDS
Probate Code Section 6806 removes one category of benefit from the escheat rules described elsewhere in this sheet: a benefit of money or other property distributable from a trust established under a plan providing health and welfare, pension, vacation, severance, retirement, death, unemployment insurance, or similar benefits does not escheat to the state under this part, and instead goes back to the trust or fund it would have been paid from, subject to Code of Civil Procedure Section 1521. Section 6806 also states the reverse of this carve-out: if the plan itself has already terminated and its trust or fund has already been distributed to the plan's beneficiaries before the estate's own distribution of the unclaimed benefit occurs, then the carve-out no longer applies, and the benefit passes to, and escheats to, the state under this part after all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, a benefit consisting of money or other property distributable from a trust established under a plan providing health and welfare, pension, vacation, severance, retirement benefit, death benefit, unemployment insurance or similar benefits does not pass to or escheat to the state under this part but goes to the trust or fund from which it is distributable, subject to the provisions of Section 1521 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6806 (California Legislative Information text), Probate Code, employee benefit plan carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6806.)
  "However, if such plan has terminated and the trust or fund has been distributed to the beneficiaries thereof prior to distribution of such benefit from the estate, such benefit passes to the state and escheats to the state under this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6806 (California Legislative Information text), Probate Code, reversion of the carve-out on plan termination (this is the same Section 6806 quoted immediately above, not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6806.)
  Known gap: Section 6806 cross-references Code of Civil Procedure Section 1521 without restating its terms here; this sheet does not independently verify what Section 1521 requires or whether a given benefit plan and its trust or fund meet this carve-out's description.

THE ATTORNEY GENERAL'S ESCHEAT PROCEEDING
Escheat under Probate Code Section 6800 happens automatically at death as a matter of law, but establishing it in a way that can be enforced against property requires a court proceeding. Code of Civil Procedure Section 1420(a) gives the Attorney General authority — not before two years have passed after the decedent's death — to commence a proceeding on the state's behalf in the Superior Court for the County of Sacramento, by filing a petition, to have the state's entitlement adjudged. Section 1420(b) requires that petition to describe the property, name the person last in possession of it, name any person claiming it, and state the facts and circumstances making it escheated property. Section 1420(c) then requires the court, on the petition's filing, to order everyone interested in the estate to appear and show cause within 60 days why the estate should not vest in the state, and requires that order to be published at least once a week for four consecutive weeks in a Sacramento County newspaper, with the last publication at least 10 days before the hearing date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "At any time after two years after the death of any decedent who leaves property to which the state is entitled by reason of it having escheated to the state, the Attorney General shall commence a proceeding on behalf of the state in the Superior Court for the County of Sacramento to have it adjudged that the state is so entitled. The action shall be commenced by filing a petition, which shall be treated as the information elsewhere referred to in this title."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(a) (California Legislative Information text), Code of Civil Procedure, two-year wait and petition to Sacramento County Superior Court (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1420.)
  "The petition shall set forth a description of the property, the name of the person last in possession thereof, the name of the person, if any, claiming the property, or portion thereof, and the facts and circumstances by virtue of which it is claimed the property has escheated."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(b) (California Legislative Information text), Code of Civil Procedure, required petition contents (this is subdivision (b) of the same Section 1420 quoted above, not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1420.)
  "Upon the filing of the petition, the court shall make an order requiring all persons interested in the estate to appear and show cause, if any, within 60 days from the date of the order, why the estate should not vest in the state. The order must be published at least once a week for four consecutive weeks in a newspaper published in the County of Sacramento, the last publication to be at least 10 days prior to the date set for the hearing."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(c) (California Legislative Information text), Code of Civil Procedure, order to show cause and publication (this is subdivision (c) of the same Section 1420 quoted above, not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1420.)
  Known gap: Section 1420 sets the Attorney General's authority and the petition and publication requirements; it does not obligate the Attorney General to commence a proceeding on any particular estate within any deadline, and this sheet does not report whether such a proceeding has been filed regarding any specific decedent's property.

INTERACTION WITH AN EXISTING PROBATE ADMINISTRATION
When a probate administration for the decedent's estate is already open, Section 1420(d) provides a path to distribution without a separate escheat lawsuit: if no one entitled to succeed to the property has appeared and claimed it before the decree of final distribution (or before the Attorney General commences a proceeding), or if the court finds that anyone who did appear is not entitled to it, the probate court itself — upon final settlement of the administration, after paying all debts and expenses — distributes the remaining money and property to the State of California. Separately, Section 1420(e) gives the Attorney General authority to direct the public administrator to commence estate administration if no administration proceeding has been commenced within six months of the decedent's death, so that an estate with no known heirs does not simply sit unadministered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If proceedings for the administration of any estate of the decedent have been instituted and none of the persons entitled to succeed thereto have appeared and made claim to the property, or any portion thereof, before the decree of final distribution therein is made, or before the commencement of a proceeding by the Attorney General, or if the court shall find that the persons as have appeared are not entitled to the property of the estate, or any portion thereof, the court shall, upon final settlement of the proceedings for the administration of the estate, after the payment of all debts and expenses of administration, distribute all moneys and other property remaining to the State of California."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(d) (California Legislative Information text), Code of Civil Procedure, distribution to the state at final settlement of a pending administration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1420.)
  "If proceedings for the administration of any estate have not been commenced within six months from the death of any decedent the Attorney General may direct the public administrator to commence the same forthwith."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(e) (California Legislative Information text), Code of Civil Procedure, Attorney General may direct public administrator to commence administration (this is subdivision (e) of the same Section 1420 quoted above, not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1420.)
  Known gap: Section 1420(d) describes what the probate court does once administration is under way and no claimant has appeared or prevailed; it does not itself say when a probate case must be opened for an estate with no known heirs in the first place, apart from the six-month administration-referral trigger in subdivision (e) that this clause also describes.

A KNOWN HEIR'S OR LEGATEE'S SHARE THAT IS NEVER COLLECTED
The rules described elsewhere in this sheet address estates with no known heirs at all. A related but distinct rule addresses money or property that was distributed to a known heir, legatee, or devisee — identified and entitled — but that the person simply never collected. Under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1444, when such distributed money or property has been deposited in a county treasury to the credit of known heirs, legatees, or devisees (or remains on deposit to the credit of an estate after final distribution to them), it is not held there indefinitely: at the next county settlement following the expiration of one year from the date of that deposit, it is paid over to the State Treasurer or Controller, as provided in the statute's Chapter 2 receipt-and-deposit provisions, placing it on the same unclaimed-property track as other escheated funds.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "At the time of the next county settlement following the expiration of one year from the date of its deposit in the county treasury, all money or other property distributed in the administration of an estate of a deceased person and heretofore or hereafter deposited in the county treasury to the credit of known heirs, legatees, or devisees, and any money or other property remaining on deposit to the credit of an estate after final distribution to such known heirs, legatees or devisees, shall be paid to the Treasurer or Controller as provided in Chapter 2."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1444 (California Legislative Information text), Code of Civil Procedure, uncollected known-distributee shares transferred to the state after one year (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1444.)
  Known gap: Section 1444 sets the one-year county-treasury holding period and the county settlement mechanism for transfer to the state; it does not itself restate the notice a known distributee may have received before the deposit, nor the further claim rights and permanent-escheat timeline described elsewhere in this sheet that apply once the funds reach the state.

THE FIVE-YEAR WINDOW BEFORE ESCHEAT BECOMES PERMANENT
An initial escheat judgment does not permanently close the door to a later claim. Code of Civil Procedure Section 1430(a) provides that property covered by an escheat proceeding permanently escheats to the state only upon the expiration of five years after entry of judgment in the proceeding (or, for a notice-by-publication escheat action under Section 1415, five years after the publication is completed) — except as subdivision (b) provides. Section 1430(b) preserves a claim right during that five-year window, and even afterward in a limited sense, for infants and persons of unsound mind born before the five-year period expires, subject to a presumption (rebuttable only by the person appearing and claiming) that no such person exists, a presumption that is conclusive in favor of a good-faith purchaser from the state. Section 1430(c) separately lets a named beneficiary of the escheated property — or, if that beneficiary is dead or adjudicated dead, a blood relative of the beneficiary — claim the property at any time within the same five-year period following judgment, with entitlement to immediate payment, subject to an exception for a person whose interest was specifically restricted or barred by the donating or transferring instrument.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Upon the expiration of five years after the date of entry of judgment in any proceeding pursuant to this chapter, or upon the expiration of five years after completion of notice by publication in an escheat action taken pursuant to Section 1415, the property covered by that proceeding or action shall permanently escheat to the state, except as provided in subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1430(a) (California Legislative Information text), Code of Civil Procedure, five-year permanent escheat trigger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1430.)
  "Infants and persons of unsound mind shall have the right to appear and claim such property as provided in this title if born before the expiration of the five-year period; but it shall be presumed that there are no infants nor persons of unsound mind who are or will be entitled to claim this property unless and until they appear and claim the property as provided in this title."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1430(b) (California Legislative Information text), Code of Civil Procedure, infant/unsound-mind claim right (this is subdivision (b) of the same Section 1430 quoted above, not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1430.)
  "a named beneficiary of property that escheats pursuant to this title or, if the beneficiary is deceased or a court renders a judgment that the beneficiary is dead, a blood relative of the named beneficiary may claim property described in subdivision (a) at any time within five years after the date of entry of judgment in any proceeding under this chapter."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1430(c) (California Legislative Information text), Code of Civil Procedure, named-beneficiary/blood-relative claim right (this is subdivision (c) of the same Section 1430 quoted above, not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1430.)
  Known gap: Section 1430 measures its five-year period from entry of judgment in 'any proceeding pursuant to this chapter' or from completion of Section 1415 publication; it does not itself specify which of the several escheat-proceeding paths described elsewhere in this sheet (the Attorney General's Section 1420 petition, or distribution within a pending probate administration under Section 1420(d)) produces the 'judgment' that starts this clock for a given estate.

WHERE PERMANENTLY ESCHEATED PROPERTY ULTIMATELY GOES
Once property permanently escheats under the five-year rule, Code of Civil Procedure Section 1431 directs its final disposition within state accounts. Money that was held in the Unclaimed Property Fund and has become permanently escheated is transferred, on the Controller's order, to the General Fund. Property other than money that was held by the Controller or Treasurer in an Unclaimed Property Fund account and has become permanently escheated is not physically transferred but is instead re-recorded: the Controller's and Treasurer's records are adjusted to show it held in the name of the General Fund.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "When money in the Unclaimed Property Fund has become permanently escheated to the state, the amount thereof shall, on order of the Controller, be transferred to the General Fund. When property other than money held by the Controller or Treasurer in the name of any account in the Unclaimed Property Fund has become permanently escheated to the state, the records of the Controller and Treasurer shall be adjusted to show that such property is held in the name of the General Fund."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1431 (California Legislative Information text), Code of Civil Procedure, transfer to the General Fund (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1431.)
  Known gap: Section 1431 governs only the bookkeeping disposition of property already permanently escheated under Section 1430; it does not affect, extend, or shorten the claim rights that Section 1430 itself preserves for infants, persons of unsound mind, or named beneficiaries and their blood relatives.

(3) This state has the right to escheat and take intangible property being administered as part of a decedent’s estate in that jurisdiction if the decedent was domiciled in this state at the time of the decedent’s death.

expectedJSON.gap: These sections turn on 'domicile,' a legal concept the statute does not define here and that can be genuinely contested where a decedent had connections to more than one state; this sheet does not determine any decedent's domicile.

expectedJSON.body: Probate Code Section 6806 removes one category of benefit from the escheat rules described elsewhere in this sheet: a benefit of money or other property distributable from a trust established under a plan providing health and welfare, pension, vacation, severance, retirement, death, unemployment insurance, or similar benefits does not escheat to the state under this part, and instead goes back to the trust or fund it would have been paid from, subject to Code of Civil Procedure Section 1521. Section 6806 also states the reverse of this carve-out: if the plan itself has already terminated and its trust or fund has already been distributed to the plan's beneficiaries before the estate's own distribution of the unclaimed benefit occurs, then the carve-out no longer applies, and the benefit passes to, and escheats to, the state under this part after all.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6806 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Probate Code, employee benefit plan carve-out
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, a benefit consisting of money or other property distributable from a trust established under a plan providing health and welfare, pension, vacation, severance, retirement benefit, death benefit, unemployment insurance or similar benefits does not pass to or escheat to the state under this part but goes to the trust or fund from which it is distributable, subject to the provisions of Section 1521 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6806 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Probate Code, reversion of the carve-out on plan termination (this is the same Section 6806 quoted immediately above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: However, if such plan has terminated and the trust or fund has been distributed to the beneficiaries thereof prior to distribution of such benefit from the estate, such benefit passes to the state and escheats to the state under this part.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 6806 cross-references Code of Civil Procedure Section 1521 without restating its terms here; this sheet does not independently verify what Section 1521 requires or whether a given benefit plan and its trust or fund meet this carve-out's description.

expectedJSON.body: Escheat under Probate Code Section 6800 happens automatically at death as a matter of law, but establishing it in a way that can be enforced against property requires a court proceeding. Code of Civil Procedure Section 1420(a) gives the Attorney General authority — not before two years have passed after the decedent's death — to commence a proceeding on the state's behalf in the Superior Court for the County of Sacramento, by filing a petition, to have the state's entitlement adjudged. Section 1420(b) requires that petition to describe the property, name the person last in possession of it, name any person claiming it, and state the facts and circumstances making it escheated property. Section 1420(c) then requires the court, on the petition's filing, to order everyone interested in the estate to appear and show cause within 60 days why the estate should not vest in the state, and requires that order to be published at least once a week for four consecutive weeks in a Sacramento County newspaper, with the last publication at least 10 days before the hearing date.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, two-year wait and petition to Sacramento County Superior Court
citations.quote: At any time after two years after the death of any decedent who leaves property to which the state is entitled by reason of it having escheated to the state, the Attorney General shall commence a proceeding on behalf of the state in the Superior Court for the County of Sacramento to have it adjudged that the state is so entitled. The action shall be commenced by filing a petition, which shall be treated as the information elsewhere referred to in this title.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, required petition contents (this is subdivision (b) of the same Section 1420 quoted above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: The petition shall set forth a description of the property, the name of the person last in possession thereof, the name of the person, if any, claiming the property, or portion thereof, and the facts and circumstances by virtue of which it is claimed the property has escheated.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, order to show cause and publication (this is subdivision (c) of the same Section 1420 quoted above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: Upon the filing of the petition, the court shall make an order requiring all persons interested in the estate to appear and show cause, if any, within 60 days from the date of the order, why the estate should not vest in the state. The order must be published at least once a week for four consecutive weeks in a newspaper published in the County of Sacramento, the last publication to be at least 10 days prior to the date set for the hearing.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 1420 sets the Attorney General's authority and the petition and publication requirements; it does not obligate the Attorney General to commence a proceeding on any particular estate within any deadline, and this sheet does not report whether such a proceeding has been filed regarding any specific decedent's property.

expectedJSON.body: When a probate administration for the decedent's estate is already open, Section 1420(d) provides a path to distribution without a separate escheat lawsuit: if no one entitled to succeed to the property has appeared and claimed it before the decree of final distribution (or before the Attorney General commences a proceeding), or if the court finds that anyone who did appear is not entitled to it, the probate court itself — upon final settlement of the administration, after paying all debts and expenses — distributes the remaining money and property to the State of California. Separately, Section 1420(e) gives the Attorney General authority to direct the public administrator to commence estate administration if no administration proceeding has been commenced within six months of the decedent's death, so that an estate with no known heirs does not simply sit unadministered.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, distribution to the state at final settlement of a pending administration
citations.quote: If proceedings for the administration of any estate of the decedent have been instituted and none of the persons entitled to succeed thereto have appeared and made claim to the property, or any portion thereof, before the decree of final distribution therein is made, or before the commencement of a proceeding by the Attorney General, or if the court shall find that the persons as have appeared are not entitled to the property of the estate, or any portion thereof, the court shall, upon final settlement of the proceedings for the administration of the estate, after the payment of all debts and expenses of administration, distribute all moneys and other property remaining to the State of California.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, Attorney General may direct public administrator to commence administration (this is subdivision (e) of the same Section 1420 quoted above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: If proceedings for the administration of any estate have not been commenced within six months from the death of any decedent the Attorney General may direct the public administrator to commence the same forthwith.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 1420(d) describes what the probate court does once administration is under way and no claimant has appeared or prevailed; it does not itself say when a probate case must be opened for an estate with no known heirs in the first place, apart from the six-month administration-referral trigger in subdivision (e) that this clause also describes.

expectedJSON.body: The rules described elsewhere in this sheet address estates with no known heirs at all. A related but distinct rule addresses money or property that was distributed to a known heir, legatee, or devisee — identified and entitled — but that the person simply never collected. Under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1444, when such distributed money or property has been deposited in a county treasury to the credit of known heirs, legatees, or devisees (or remains on deposit to the credit of an estate after final distribution to them), it is not held there indefinitely: at the next county settlement following the expiration of one year from the date of that deposit, it is paid over to the State Treasurer or Controller, as provided in the statute's Chapter 2 receipt-and-deposit provisions, placing it on the same unclaimed-property track as other escheated funds.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1444 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, uncollected known-distributee shares transferred to the state after one year
citations.quote: At the time of the next county settlement following the expiration of one year from the date of its deposit in the county treasury, all money or other property distributed in the administration of an estate of a deceased person and heretofore or hereafter deposited in the county treasury to the credit of known heirs, legatees, or devisees, and any money or other property remaining on deposit to the credit of an estate after final distribution to such known heirs, legatees or devisees, shall be paid to the Treasurer or Controller as provided in Chapter 2.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 1444 sets the one-year county-treasury holding period and the county settlement mechanism for transfer to the state; it does not itself restate the notice a known distributee may have received before the deposit, nor the further claim rights and permanent-escheat timeline described elsewhere in this sheet that apply once the funds reach the state.

expectedJSON.body: An initial escheat judgment does not permanently close the door to a later claim. Code of Civil Procedure Section 1430(a) provides that property covered by an escheat proceeding permanently escheats to the state only upon the expiration of five years after entry of judgment in the proceeding (or, for a notice-by-publication escheat action under Section 1415, five years after the publication is completed) — except as subdivision (b) provides. Section 1430(b) preserves a claim right during that five-year window, and even afterward in a limited sense, for infants and persons of unsound mind born before the five-year period expires, subject to a presumption (rebuttable only by the person appearing and claiming) that no such person exists, a presumption that is conclusive in favor of a good-faith purchaser from the state. Section 1430(c) separately lets a named beneficiary of the escheated property — or, if that beneficiary is dead or adjudicated dead, a blood relative of the beneficiary — claim the property at any time within the same five-year period following judgment, with entitlement to immediate payment, subject to an exception for a person whose interest was specifically restricted or barred by the donating or transferring instrument.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1430(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, five-year permanent escheat trigger
citations.quote: Upon the expiration of five years after the date of entry of judgment in any proceeding pursuant to this chapter, or upon the expiration of five years after completion of notice by publication in an escheat action taken pursuant to Section 1415, the property covered by that proceeding or action shall permanently escheat to the state, except as provided in subdivision (b).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1430(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, infant/unsound-mind claim right (this is subdivision (b) of the same Section 1430 quoted above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: Infants and persons of unsound mind shall have the right to appear and claim such property as provided in this title if born before the expiration of the five-year period; but it shall be presumed that there are no infants nor persons of unsound mind who are or will be entitled to claim this property unless and until they appear and claim the property as provided in this title.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1430(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, named-beneficiary/blood-relative claim right (this is subdivision (c) of the same Section 1430 quoted above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: a named beneficiary of property that escheats pursuant to this title or, if the beneficiary is deceased or a court renders a judgment that the beneficiary is dead, a blood relative of the named beneficiary may claim property described in subdivision (a) at any time within five years after the date of entry of judgment in any proceeding under this chapter.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 1430 measures its five-year period from entry of judgment in 'any proceeding pursuant to this chapter' or from completion of Section 1415 publication; it does not itself specify which of the several escheat-proceeding paths described elsewhere in this sheet (the Attorney General's Section 1420 petition, or distribution within a pending probate administration under Section 1420(d)) produces the 'judgment' that starts this clock for a given estate.

expectedJSON.body: Once property permanently escheats under the five-year rule, Code of Civil Procedure Section 1431 directs its final disposition within state accounts. Money that was held in the Unclaimed Property Fund and has become permanently escheated is transferred, on the Controller's order, to the General Fund. Property other than money that was held by the Controller or Treasurer in an Unclaimed Property Fund account and has become permanently escheated is not physically transferred but is instead re-recorded: the Controller's and Treasurer's records are adjusted to show it held in the name of the General Fund.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1431 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, transfer to the General Fund
citations.quote: When money in the Unclaimed Property Fund has become permanently escheated to the state, the amount thereof shall, on order of the Controller, be transferred to the General Fund. When property other than money held by the Controller or Treasurer in the name of any account in the Unclaimed Property Fund has become permanently escheated to the state, the records of the Controller and Treasurer shall be adjusted to show that such property is held in the name of the General Fund.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 1431 governs only the bookkeeping disposition of property already permanently escheated under Section 1430; it does not affect, extend, or shorten the claim rights that Section 1430 itself preserves for infants, persons of unsound mind, or named beneficiaries and their blood relatives.
